exercises.title: Write Delete
exercises.task: Fill the three cases of Delete. Going down to the node is given; each call returns the new root of its subtree, and the parent reconnects itself.
hints: When you first wrote this in December, you found the parent with a separate search and changed parent.Left or parent.Right. That broke when the node to delete was the root itself. Returning the new subtree root avoids the parent entirely.
No child: return nil. One child: return that child. The parent's n.Left = Delete(…) does the rest.
Two children: copy the smallest key of the right subtree into n.Key, then delete that key from the right subtree: n.Right = Delete(n.Right, n.Key).

exercises.title: Floor: which function is running?
exercises.task: A program's functions sit one after another in memory. A profiler (D3, exercise 2) or a panic's stack trace only knows an address, the program counter; to print a name it needs the function whose code begins at the largest address ≤ pc. Keep the start addresses in a BST: that is the floor, the largest key ≤ t. (Go's runtime does this lookup with a sorted table instead of a tree, for runtime.FuncForPC.) Follow one path from the root, like Search, remembering the best candidate.
hints: If the node's key is ≤ t, it is a candidate; a better one can only be on its right.
If the node's key is > t, the answer can only be on its left.
A loop is enough: for n != nil { … }, keeping best and found.
